
The Robusta plots tell a more varied story than Arabica. ARIMAX is clearly the strongest model, tracking the observed price closely throughout the test period including the sharp acceleration from 2023, consistent with its $R^2$ of 0.926. The 95% confidence interval widens progressively toward the end of the test period, reflecting the growing uncertainty of autoregressive forecasts over longer horizons, but the observed price stays within the band for almost the entire period. MLR fails visibly, with forecasts oscillating erratically and producing large directional errors, which explains its $R^2$ of 0.276. Among the ML models, XGBoost and Random Forest both track the upward trajectory but underestimate the pace of the acceleration from mid-2023 onward. SVM follows the general trend without any particularly notable pattern in its deviations. The ANN remains the most unstable, with visible spikes at several points, though the regularisation has reduced their severity compared to the baseline specification.

#### Forecast Residuals

The residual plots below zoom in on the forecast errors for each model, making it easier to spot any systematic bias or unusual episodes that the trajectory plots might obscure. Within each variety, the y-axis scale is fixed across all panels to allow direct comparison of residual amplitude between models.

*This chunk plots the forecast residuals (predicted minus actual) for each model over the test period. A residual series hovering around zero with no systematic pattern indicates an unbiased model; persistent positive or negative deviations reveal directional bias, while increasing variance over time suggests heteroskedasticity in the forecast errors.*

```{r residuals_plots, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}

df_residuals <- bind_rows(
  df_forecasts_ara %>%
    mutate(residual = predicted - actual,
           series   = "Arabica"),
  df_forecasts_rob %>%
    mutate(residual = predicted - actual,
           series   = "Robusta")
)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PLOT 1 — ARABICA RESIDUALS
# Fixed y-axis scale across all panels to allow direct
# comparison of residual amplitude between models.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

p_res_ara <- ggplot(
  df_residuals %>% filter(series == "Arabica"),
  aes(x = date, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ifelse(residual > 0, 0, residual),
                  ymax = ifelse(residual > 0, residual, 0)),
              fill = "#8B4513", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(color = "#8B4513", linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, ncol = 3, scales = "fixed") +
  labs(title    = "Forecast residuals — Arabica futures (test set)",
       subtitle = "Residual = Predicted - Actual. Dashed line at zero.",
       x = NULL, y = "Residual (USD/lb)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f5ece6", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PLOT 2 — ROBUSTA RESIDUALS
# Fixed y-axis scale across all panels to allow direct
# comparison of residual amplitude between models.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

p_res_rob <- ggplot(
  df_residuals %>% filter(series == "Robusta"),
  aes(x = date, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ifelse(residual > 0, 0, residual),
                  ymax = ifelse(residual > 0, residual, 0)),
              fill = "#2E8B57", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(color = "#2E8B57", linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, ncol = 3, scales = "fixed") +
  labs(title    = "Forecast residuals — Robusta futures (test set)",
       subtitle = "Residual = Predicted - Actual. Dashed line at zero.",
       x = NULL, y = "Residual (USD/tonne)") +

    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#e8f5ec", color = NA),

    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  ) +

p_res_ara
p_res_rob
```

**For Arabica** : Almost all models show a pronounced negative spike just before 2022, reflecting a common failure to anticipate the sharp price peak at that point in the cycle. MLR and ANN overestimate the most at the start of the test period, while other models also show some positive bias early on but to a lesser degree. From late 2022 onward, XGBoost and Random Forest stand out with larger positive residuals than the other models, suggesting they were slow to incorporate the price decline and continued to forecast higher prices than what was actually observed. Beyond these episodes, residuals oscillate reasonably around zero for the remaining models.

**For Robusta** : ARIMAX produces the most well-behaved residuals, oscillating around zero without any persistent directional bias. Random Forest shows two distinct negative episodes: one from mid-2021 to early 2022, and another from late 2022 through 2023. MLR follows a similar pattern but concentrated mostly in 2023, with the largest negative residuals of all models during that period. XGBoost mirrors this pattern but in a less pronounced way, with residuals that dip negative but partially recover more quickly. SVM deviates significantly at times but tends to correct itself faster than the other models when it diverges. The ANN is the most unstable, with residuals that lean predominantly negative and swing sharply in both directions throughout the test period.

## Interpretation of Results

### Overall Model Performance

The out-of-sample results present a consistent and interpretable picture of predictive performance across the six model families. Two broad conclusions emerge. First, ARIMAX's explicit autoregressive structure gives it a clear edge over every other model for both varieties, confirming that the persistence of prices around their own past values is a primary source of short-run predictability that none of the five remaining models, all of which rely solely on contemporaneous exogenous predictors, can fully replicate. Second, the performance gap between the strongest and weakest models is substantially wider for Robusta than for Arabica, reflecting the shorter estimation sample, the more pronounced multicollinearity among Robusta predictors, and the sharp late-sample price acceleration discussed further below.

For Arabica, ARIMAX stands clearly apart from the rest of the field once its order is fixed on the initial training window and applied as-is throughout the walk-forward loop, reaching an out-of-sample 
$R^2$ of 0.955. XGBoost, Random Forest and SVM form a second tier close together at 0.812, 0.815 and 0.813 respectively, suggesting the three pick up much of the same signal from the predictor set rather than exploiting genuinely different information. MLR achieves $R^2 = 0.784$, a result that reflects the strong trending co-movement between Arabica prices and the macroeconomic variables in levels rather than genuine structural predictive power. The ANN trails at 0.728 for reasons discussed in the limitations section.

For Robusta, ARIMAX again delivers the strongest result at $R^2=0.926$, though the margin over the second tier is narrower than for Arabica: XGBoost follows at $R^2=0.797$, while SVM and Random Forest achieve 0.761 and 0.676 respectively. The most striking result is the collapse of MLR to $R^2 =0.276$, with forecast trajectories that oscillate erratically around the observed series and produce large directional errors. This failure reflects the well-known sensitivity of OLS to multicollinearity in short samples. With only 153 training observations and 14 highly collinear predictors, as documented in the correlation and VIF analyses, individual coefficient estimates carry high variance and are poorly identified. Under the walk-forward protocol, where the model is re-estimated from scratch at every step as the training window expands by one observation, this instability translates directly into forecasting behaviour: small changes in the training sample can shift the fitted coefficients substantially from one step to the next, producing the erratic, oscillating forecasts visible in the Robusta residual plots rather than a smooth or systematically biased error pattern. The regularisation exercise conducted as a robustness check on MLR supports this reading directly: Ridge regression, which shrinks and stabilises every coefficient without removing any predictor, nearly doubles Robusta's $R^2$ to 0.464, while the same penalty applied to Arabica's already better-behaved coefficients makes performance worse rather than better. This asymmetry is exactly what a multicollinearity-driven explanation predicts, and it confirms that Robusta's weak MLR result is a symptom of collinearity and sample size rather than a failure of the predictor set itself.

The coefficient tables from the ARIMAX training-set estimation further illuminate the challenge of identifying interpretable linear relationships in this predictor space. For both varieties, only a small number of regressors reach conventional significance thresholds: Sugar, WTI, the Federal Funds Rate and COT net MM for Arabica, and CPI, WTI and COT net MM for Robusta, with DXY approaching significance at the 10% level. This outcome is not a failure of specification but a further manifestation of the same multicollinearity problem discussed above: Production, Consumption and Exports move almost in lockstep over the sample, as the correlation matrix shows pairwise coefficients between them ranging from 0.73 to 0.94, and CPI trends closely alongside all three for the same reason. As with the MLR case, this leaves the OLS component of ARIMAX unable to isolate the individual contribution of any one of these variables, inflating standard errors and suppressing t-statistics even when the group's collective predictive content is substantial. This observation provides a retrospective justification for the machine learning approach adopted in this study: Random Forest and XGBoost are specifically designed to exploit the predictive information contained in groups of correlated variables through non-linear combinations and variable selection mechanisms that are unavailable to the linear regression component of ARIMAX.

The overall level of predictive accuracy achieved, with $R^2$ values generally above 0.75 across the best-performing models for both varieties, is worth noting in context. These results are obtained on series in levels, and the co-trending of prices with macroeconomic variables may inflate $R^2$ beyond what would be achievable on stationary first-differenced series. This point is addressed explicitly in the limitations section.

### The Role of Financial and Speculative Variables

The permutation importance analysis, computed across all four machine learning models rather than any single one, provides the clearest picture of which predictors drive out-of-sample accuracy, and the consistency of the ranking across four structurally different model families is what makes it informative rather than an artefact of one particular architecture. For Arabica, Ending stocks ranks among the top three predictors for all four ML models (contributing a ΔMSE of 0.045 for Random Forest alone, by some margin its largest single predictor), the single most consistent finding in the comparison. COT net Managed Money follows closely, ranking top three for three of the four models, and WTI for three of the four as well, though not always the same three. The dominance of speculative positioning is consistent with the progressive financialisation of commodity futures markets more broadly: the net position of Managed Money participants captures market-wide expectations about future price direction that are not yet reflected in contemporaneous fundamentals. The strong predictive power of COT net MM at the one-month-ahead horizon suggests that this sentiment signal is not fully incorporated into current prices, creating a forecasting opportunity that the tree-based and kernel models exploit through their non-linear variable interactions. Sugar No.1 prices feature prominently for the ANN in particular, consistent with the strong co-movement between the two series already documented in the correlation analysis (0.71, the highest pairwise price correlation observed in this study) and with the direct supply-side link between coffee and sugar cultivation in Brazil, the world's largest producer of both crops. A plausible interpretation is that shifts in the relative profitability of the two crops are anticipated by market participants and reflected in coffee futures prices before they appear in realised production data, though this study does not test this mechanism directly and the finding is limited to the observed correlation and the variable's contribution to forecast accuracy.

The mechanics of the COT signal also point to a feedback structure worth making explicit. A positive net Managed Money position reflects funds that have already taken long positions in anticipation of rising prices. If that buying pressure itself contributes to the price increase, as the positive and significant COT coefficient in both the MLR and ARIMAX specifications suggests, the resulting price rise could in principle reinforce the original bullish positioning rather than simply confirming it. This self-reinforcing dynamic would be consistent with what the permutation importance results show, namely that COT net MM contributes meaningfully to several of the ML models' one-month-ahead forecasts. However, the present analysis cannot speak to this mechanism directly: walk-forward forecasting accuracy and a positive coefficient sign are compatible with a self-reinforcing dynamic, but neither result is designed to test for one, and no claim of this kind is made here beyond noting that the observed coefficient sign and forecasting contribution do not rule it out. The lagged-COT robustness check conducted later in this study, which adds COT net MM at one, two and three months back to the baseline predictor set, offers a further piece of evidence here: the lagged values do not meaningfully improve one-month-ahead forecasts for most models, suggesting that whatever information the lags carry is already implicitly absorbed by the contemporaneous COT variable, which is a more parsimonious result than a genuine multi-period feedback loop would imply, though it does not settle the question either way.

For Robusta, the importance hierarchy differs from Arabica in its upper ranks. The Federal Funds Rate is the standout result here: it ranks in the top three for all four ML models, the strongest consensus finding for this variety, and WTI ranks first specifically for three of the four models. The stronger role of energy costs is consistent with the production geography of Robusta: cultivation is concentrated in a small number of countries, chiefly Vietnam and Indonesia, compared to the twelve countries that contribute to the Arabica indices in this study, so country-specific shocks to production and logistics costs plausibly translate more directly into aggregate price movements. The consistency of the Federal Funds Rate is worth reading alongside the partial dependence results discussed earlier in this study: the rate sat close to zero with limited variation for most of the 2008–2021 period before climbing sharply from 2022 onward, and this later regime coincides closely with the test period used to evaluate the models. A predictor whose behaviour shifts so markedly within the window being forecast is well placed to carry genuine one-month-ahead signal, even where the partial dependence shape itself is not always the smooth, monotonic relationship that a simple monetary policy channel would predict.

Two patterns stand out across both varieties. First, the two most consistently important predictors identified across all four ML models, Ending stocks for Arabica and the Federal Funds Rate for Robusta, both belong to categories, USDA fundamentals and monetary policy respectively, that are not obviously "financial positioning" in the narrow sense, suggesting that the informative variables differ by variety rather than falling into one single dominant category. Second, as the next section discusses, climate variables sit consistently in the lower half of the ranking for both varieties, though not always in the very last positions. This finding carries a practical implication: short-run price signals for coffee are not reliably captured by any single category of predictor, but the specific variables that matter, inventory levels for Arabica, energy and interest rate conditions for Robusta, are worth monitoring directly rather than assuming climate or supply data alone will suffice at monthly frequency.

### Climate Variables and the Lag Structure Problem

A consistent finding across both varieties is that the two national climate indices, Precipitation and Temperature, tend to rank in the lower half of the importance ranking on average, though not uniformly: Precipitation ranks as high as fifth of fourteen for XGBoost on Arabica, and Temperature as high as sixth and seventh for XGBoost and ANN on Robusta respectively. Averaged across all eight model-variety combinations, Precipitation sits at rank 9.1 of 14 and Temperature at 9.6, both below the midpoint but with enough variation across models that neither variable is reliably at the bottom of the ranking.

This weak showing should not be interpreted as evidence that climate is irrelevant to coffee prices. Rather, it plausibly reflects a mismatch between the one-step-ahead monthly forecasting horizon of the models and the lag structure through which climate is understood to affect prices. Coffee cherries typically take around six to nine months to ripen after flowering, depending on variety, altitude and growing conditions, so a climate shock during the flowering or fruit-development stage would not show up in realised production until several months later, and would only affect prices with a further lag as any resulting supply shortfall propagates through inventories and trade flows. A contemporaneous monthly model is not designed to capture this kind of delayed transmission directly. One plausible consequence is that the climate signal is partly absorbed by the production and ending stocks variables, which reflect realised supply outcomes rather than the weather conditions that produced them, though this study does not test that specific channel directly and the climate variables' low importance scores could equally reflect the national-average climate resolution limitation discussed in the Climate Data Resolution section.

The ONI index does not offer as clean a counter-example as might be expected. For Arabica, ONI ranks reasonably high for two of the four models (fourth for both Random Forest and XGBoost) but only middling for the other two (ninth for SVM, fifth for ANN), so at best a partial signal that ENSO conditions carry more expectational weight than realised local weather. For Robusta, the pattern runs the other way entirely: ONI is the single least important predictor of all fourteen for both Random Forest and XGBoost, and only middling for SVM and ANN. Whatever role expectation formation around El Niño and La Niña episodes might play in Arabica pricing, evidently it does not extend to Robusta in this analysis, and no attempt is made here to explain why the two varieties would differ on this specific channel; the result is reported as observed rather than rationalised after the fact.

### Arabica vs Robusta: Structural Differences

The contrast between Arabica and Robusta results across models reveals structural differences between the two markets that go beyond the shorter sample available for Robusta, though the ARIMAX result in particular now needs to be read carefully in light of the order-fixing exercise conducted in this study.

Under the fixed-order specification, ARIMAX now performs better for Arabica ($R^2 = 0.955$, ARIMA(2,0,1)) than for Robusta ($R^2= 0.926$, ARIMA(1,0,3)), the reverse of the ranking obtained when the order was re-selected at every walk-forward step. This reversal is informative in its own right. Fixing the order via a single, thorough search on the full initial training window removed a source of noise that appears to have disproportionately affected Arabica under the earlier, re-adaptive specification, plausibly because that specification occasionally selected an unstable or under-specified order on the smaller training windows encountered early in the walk-forward loop. Robusta's result, by contrast, barely moved between the two specifications, suggesting its autoregressive structure was already being captured reasonably well even without fixing the order. Both series still carry meaningful short-run autocorrelation, as reflected in the richer moving-average component retained for Robusta (an MA(3) term) against the two autoregressive terms retained for Arabica, but the practical gain from the methodological change discussed in this study accrued mostly to Arabica rather than to Robusta.

The failure of MLR on Robusta but not Arabica is partly a sample size effect, with 153 versus 168 training observations, but also reflects the more pronounced multicollinearity among Robusta predictors already documented in the VIF diagnostics, where Production, Consumption, Exports and CPI all trend upward together over the shorter 2008–2023 window available for this variety. With fewer training observations to begin with, this shared trend leaves OLS even less able to separate the individual contribution of each predictor than it is for Arabica, where the same trending variables are estimated over a longer 2006–2023 window. The regularisation results reported above sharpen this contrast further: Ridge nearly doubles Robusta's $R^2$ while making Arabica's worse, which is difficult to explain by sample size alone and points instead to a genuine difference in how entangled the two varieties' predictors are with one another.

The relatively weaker performance of tree-based models on Robusta, with Random Forest at $R^2 = 0.676$ and XGBoost at 0.797 compared to their Arabica counterparts of 0.815 and 0.812, reflects the extrapolation limitation of ensemble methods. Random Forest and XGBoost average over training observations and cannot produce predictions that substantially exceed the range of target values seen during training. The sharp upward acceleration in Robusta prices from mid-2023 onward moves beyond the price range of the training set, causing both models to produce forecasts that flatten while the observed series continues rising. This limitation is clearly visible in the forecast trajectory and residual plots, where a persistent negative bias emerges for both tree-based models from late 2022 onward.

### Robustness of the Methodology

Four robustness checks were conducted alongside the main results: disaggregating the climate indices into their national components, restricting predictors to variety-specific producing countries, testing OECD GDP growth at quarterly frequency, and adding lagged COT positioning to the baseline specification. Two additional tuning extensions, cost-complexity pruning for Random Forest and a single pruned CART tree, speak to the same question from a narrower angle. Read together, these checks paint a fairly consistent picture: the modelling choices made throughout this study tend to hold up well, and where a check does move the results, it usually does so for a reason that fits the rest of the analysis rather than against it.

Replacing the two production-weighted climate indices with their 28 underlying national series is the clearest case. Every one of the eight model-variety combinations gets worse, sometimes only mildly for Random Forest and XGBoost, but severely enough for SVM and ANN that both produce negative $R^2$ values. With 40 regressors and only around 170 training observations, this is exactly the kind of overparameterisation the curse of dimensionality would predict, and it also fits a more substantive story: aggregating by production weight averages out country-specific noise that has little to do with how the global market actually prices coffee. The check validates the aggregation approach on both counts at once.

Restricting the predictors to variety-specific producing countries tells a more divided story. For Robusta, it helps: four of the six models improve, and XGBoost reaches its best result anywhere in this study at $R^2=0.849$. That makes sense, since the global indices otherwise dilute Robusta's signal with conditions in countries, like most Arabica producers, that grow essentially none of it. For Arabica, the opposite happens, and every model gets worse. The reason is more structural than contradictory: Brazil alone already dominates the global indices with such a large production weight that narrowing the country list barely changes Arabica's climate signal, while it does strip out Robusta-producing countries whose consumption and export activity still matters for the fundamentals variables. The two varieties respond differently not because the logic is inconsistent, but because their production geography is genuinely asymmetric.

The GDP growth check is the most straightforwardly negative of the four. Simply moving to quarterly frequency already hurts most models, ANN worst of all, collapsing to a strongly negative $R^2$ for Arabica. Once frequency is held fixed, adding GDP growth itself does little either way, and where it helps at all the gain is small and inconsistent across models. This is not a surprising result once CPI, the Federal Funds Rate, world consumption and the dollar index are already in the model: GDP growth has little left to add at this frequency, and since it only exists quarterly, testing it at all means paying the cost of a lower-frequency specification whether or not the variable itself turns out to matter.

The lagged COT check was motivated by a question raised earlier in the discussion of speculative positioning: if Managed Money's net position both reflects and reinforces price expectations, does its recent history carry information the contemporaneous value does not? The evidence here says mostly no. Six of the eight model-variety combinations get worse when COT lagged by one, two and three months is added, and the two that improve do so only modestly. This fits the same dimensionality logic as the climate check: lagged values of the same series are highly autocorrelated with each other and with the contemporaneous position, so adding them inflates the input space without adding much genuinely new signal, at a cost the limited training samples can ill afford. None of this rules out a self-reinforcing dynamic between positioning and prices, but it does suggest that whatever information the recent past carries is already absorbed by the current position.

The two tuning extensions add a narrower but useful piece to this picture. Testing scikit-learn's `ccp_alpha` parameter on Random Forest confirms that cost-complexity pruning is not fundamentally incompatible with an ensemble of trees, as an unpruned forest reproduces the R baseline closely, but that applying it at all is actively harmful: even a mild penalty collapses performance, and a moderate one drives $R^2$ deeply negative for Robusta and close to zero for Arabica. The explanation is not a contradiction so much as a reminder of what pruning is actually for. It exists to stop a single tree, which has no ensemble to lean on, from overfitting its own training sample; forcing every tree in a Random Forest toward that same simplicity strips out the diversity the ensemble depends on to average its errors away, without solving a problem the ensemble did not have in the first place. A single pruned CART tree tested on its own performs considerably worse than the Random Forest for both varieties, which reaches the same conclusion from the other direction.

## Limitations
### Non-Stationarity and Spurious Regression

The most significant methodological limitation of this study concerns how the machine learning models handle non-stationarity. The stationarity analysis established that most variables, including both dependent price series and most macroeconomic and fundamental predictors, are integrated of order one. ARIMAX deals with this on its own terms, through the differencing parameter `auto.arima()` selects, and the fact that both final specifications end up with $d=0$ simply means the regression component already absorbs the common trend before any differencing would be needed. The ML models have no such built-in mechanism. Estimating them on levels rather than first differences opens the door to spurious regression: two series that are both trending upward will produce a high $R^2$ together even if there is no real relationship between them at all.

The reason for sticking with levels was empirical rather than a matter of convenience: first-differenced specifications came back with $R^2$ values close to zero, confirming that month-to-month price changes are close to unpredictable at this frequency. That makes the levels-based approach defensible in practice, since what the models are picking up is genuine trending co-movement between economically linked series rather than a coincidence between two unrelated ones. But it does mean the reported $R^2$ values for the ML models partly reflect that shared trend rather than a clean measure of how well the models forecast price dynamics on their own. A cointegration-based specification, modelling the long-run equilibrium between prices and fundamentals while correcting for short-run deviations, would be a natural way to address this in future work.

### ANN Instability

The Artificial Neural Network exhibits notable instability across several dimensions beyond the walk-forward re-estimation setting itself, and the extension work conducted on this model in this study makes clear that the instability is not fully resolved by any single fix. With only approximately 170 training observations at the early test steps and a compact architecture selected by time series cross-validation, the network is susceptible to converging to local minima that produce extreme predictions for isolated observations. A fixed random seed partially mitigates but does not eliminate this problem, as the loss landscape of a feedforward network contains multiple local optima of varying quality.

Depth compounds this instability rather than resolving it. Testing the network at greater depth via `neuralnet`, which has no weight decay mechanism, produces a monotonic collapse in out-of-sample $R^2$ for both varieties as more layers are added, turning negative for Robusta by five layers and for Arabica by ten. Attempting to reintroduce regularisation at depth via `RSNNS`, the only package tested here that supports both multiple hidden layers and weight decay simultaneously, made results uniformly worse rather than better, most likely because the optimiser required to access weight decay in that package is considerably less efficient than the Adam optimiser used for the single-layer ANN and its Keras extension, rather than because regularisation itself is unhelpful at depth. The choice of activation function adds a further layer of sensitivity: sigmoid and tanh produce meaningfully different results, and which one performs better for a given variety depends on the optimiser and package used to fit the network rather than on a stable property of the activation function alone. Taken together, these results suggest that the ANN's instability in this study is not solely a matter of random initialisation, but reflects a broader sensitivity of small feedforward networks, fit on a limited monthly sample, to architectural and implementation choices that are considerably less consequential for the tree-based and kernel models tested alongside it. More robust implementations would require ensemble averaging across multiple random initialisations, a consistent regularisation and optimisation framework tested jointly rather than package by package, or recurrent architectures such as Long Short-Term Memory networks that are specifically designed for sequential data and maintain a hidden state across time steps rather than reinitialising at each walk-forward step.

### Hyperparameter Sensitivity

The hyperparameter tuning throughout this study never fully nests within the walk-forward loop. Some specifications, Arabica's SVM among them, still rely on the original single chronological 80/20 split of the initial training window. Others, extended later via time series cross-validation for XGBoost, SVM and ANN, average across three chronological splits instead. Either way, the selected hyperparameters minimise error on a fixed set of validation windows rather than across the full range of training window sizes the walk-forward loop actually encounters.

The isolated neuron-count sensitivity analysis conducted for the ANN illustrates the fragility this can introduce. At Robusta's selected regularisation strength, validation error jumps more than fourfold between two and three hidden neurons before falling back down at larger widths, a pattern far more consistent with an isolated poor local optimum reached during training at that specific width than with a genuine, monotonic relationship between network size and performance. The two-neuron architecture remains the best choice for both varieties regardless, but the episode is a reminder that small feedforward networks evaluated on a limited number of validation splits can produce results whose fine-grained shape reflects the specific random initialisation encountered as much as the architecture being tested. Retaining the tuned architecture is nonetheless the methodologically consistent choice, since selecting hyperparameters based on test set performance would violate the walk-forward validation protocol, but this result highlights the importance of more robust tuning procedures, and of not over-interpreting small differences between adjacent configurations.

### Climate Data Resolution

The national climate averages used to construct the production-weighted indices are computed as simple arithmetic means across all ADM1 regions within each country, without intra-country production weights. This implies that non-producing or lightly-producing regions contribute as much to the national average as the country's main producing areas, which can attenuate the climate signal in countries where coffee cultivation is concentrated in only part of the national territory. Sub-national production data at the ADM1 level are not systematically available from the USDA FAS PSD database, making intra-country production weighting infeasible with the data collected for this study. Future work could address this using remote sensing-based estimates of coffee cultivation area at high spatial resolution to construct more targeted intra-country weights.

### Data Availability Constraints

Two structural data gaps restrict the estimation sample for certain model specifications. The CFTC Disaggregated COT report was introduced in June 2006, and since the net Managed Money position is one of the 14 predictors used throughout this study, every model, Arabica included, is in practice estimated from June 2006 onward rather than from the start of the full 2000–2023 dataset, reducing the Arabica estimation sample to 211 monthly observations. Robusta futures prices are a further constraint on top of this, available only from January 2008, which cuts the Robusta estimation sample down further still to 192 monthly observations. Both gaps are handled by restricting estimation to complete-case sub-samples, but they imply that the models in this study, and Robusta's in particular, are estimated over a considerably shorter window than the 2000–2023 period used for the exploratory and stationarity analyses earlier in this document.

### Static Model Specifications

All six models assume a static relationship between coffee prices and their predictors, with coefficients or feature importances that are fixed over time or re-estimated on an expanding window that treats all historical observations equally. This assumption is at odds with the structural changes documented in the coffee market over the analysis period, including the progressive financialisation of commodity markets from the mid-2000s onward, the post-2008 shift in monetary policy regimes, and the supply chain disruptions of the COVID-19 period. Time-varying parameter models, such as rolling-window ML specifications with a fixed rather than expanding training window, would allow predictor relationships to evolve over time and may improve performance in structurally shifting environments.

### ARIMAX Order Selection on a Single Training Window

The ARIMAX specification used throughout this study fixes its $(p,d,q)$ order once, via an exhaustive AICc-based search on the initial training window, and holds that order fixed for the remainder of the walk-forward loop, re-estimating only the coefficients as the window expands. This is a deliberate methodological choice, intended to test whether an order chosen from one sample generalises to unseen data rather than allowing the model structure itself to adapt at every step, and the resulting residual diagnostics support it: the ACF and PACF of the reference model's residuals show no material autocorrelation left uncaptured for either variety, and the residuals test as stationary under both the ADF and KPSS criteria. The limitation this introduces is more subtle than residual autocorrelation. The selected order, ARIMA(2,0,1) for Arabica and ARIMA(1,0,3) for Robusta, is optimal for the specific 168- or 153-month window used to initialise the walk-forward loop, not a universally correct specification for the full sample; a different initial training window could plausibly have yielded a different order. The search itself was also bounded, at a maximum autoregressive and moving-average order of five and a maximum differencing order of two, for computational tractability, so an even wider search conducted on the same window cannot be ruled out to yield a different result. Future work could test the sensitivity of the walk-forward results to the choice of initial window, for instance by re-running the order selection from a different starting point in the sample, to establish how much of the strong Arabica result in particular depends on the specific window used.

# Conclusion

This study estimated six forecasting models, two econometric benchmarks in the form of ARIMAX and Multiple Linear Regression and four machine learning algorithms comprising Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine and Artificial Neural Network, applied to monthly Arabica and Robusta coffee futures prices over the 2000–2023 period. Using a walk-forward expanding window validation protocol with an 80/20 train/test split, all models were evaluated on three out-of-sample metrics across a rich predictor set spanning macroeconomic, fundamental, climatic and speculative variables.

The principal empirical finding is that ARIMAX, with its $(p,d,q)$ order fixed on the initial training window and applied unchanged throughout the walk-forward loop, emerges as the strongest model for both coffee varieties, achieving out-of-sample $R^2$ values of 0.955 for Arabica and 0.926 for Robusta. XGBoost forms the strongest of the remaining models, at 0.812 for Arabica and 0.797 for Robusta, demonstrating that gradient boosting can identify non-linear relationships among predictors that the linear regression component of ARIMAX cannot accommodate, even as ARIMAX's own autoregressive structure captures the persistence in prices that a cross-sectional model like MLR cannot. The Multiple Linear Regression benchmark performs reasonably well for Arabica but collapses for Robusta at $R^2=0.276$, and the regularisation exercise conducted alongside it confirms that this collapse is driven by multicollinearity among a short sample of predictors rather than by a lack of genuine information in the predictor set: Ridge regression nearly doubles Robusta's $R^2$ while leaving Arabica's essentially unchanged or slightly worse.

The variable importance analysis, computed consistently across all four machine learning models, shows that the most informative predictors differ by variety rather than falling into one single dominant category. For Arabica, Ending stocks, COT net Managed Money and WTI are the most consistently important predictors, reflecting inventory dynamics, the financialisation of the coffee futures market, and the energy cost channel respectively. For Robusta, WTI and the Federal Funds Rate lead, plausibly linked to Robusta's more concentrated production geography and to the sharp shift in the interest rate regime that coincides with the test period used to evaluate the models. Climate variables contribute relatively little predictive power at the one-month-ahead forecasting horizon, a finding consistent with the lag, typically six to nine months, between a climate shock during flowering or fruit development and its eventual effect on realised production and, in turn, prices. This is not evidence that climate is irrelevant to coffee prices, but rather that a contemporaneous monthly model is not designed to capture this delayed transmission.

The four robustness checks and the model-specific tuning extensions conducted in this study yield several findings of independent interest. The disaggregated climate check confirms that the production-weighted aggregation of climate indices is the appropriate specification, since replacing the two global indices with 28 individual national series systematically worsens performance across all ML models. The variety-specific check reveals an important asymmetry: restricting climate and supply variables to the six Robusta-producing countries improves performance for four of the six models, with XGBoost reaching its strongest result at $R^2=0.849$, while the same restriction uniformly deteriorates Arabica performance because the global indices are already dominated by Arabica-producing countries. The GDP growth check provides no support for including this variable as a predictor, and the lagged COT check provides little support for the idea that recent speculative positioning history improves one-month-ahead forecasts beyond what the contemporaneous position already captures. Separately, the Random Forest pruning exercise confirms that cost-complexity pruning is technically compatible with an ensemble of trees, contrary to what the absence of a cp argument in R's `randomForest` might suggest, but that applying it is nonetheless harmful, since it removes the diversity across trees that the ensemble's averaging step relies on.

Several limitations constrain the interpretation of these results. Estimating ML models on non-stationary price levels raises the risk of spurious correlations driven by common trends. The ANN exhibits instability that persists across random initialisation, network depth, activation function and the specific package and optimiser used to fit it, a pattern discussed at length in this study's ANN extension work. The hyperparameter tuning procedure for SVM and ANN relies on a limited number of validation splits rather than a fully nested walk-forward search, which can leave small architectural differences reflecting a particular training run rather than a stable ranking. The national climate averages do not account for the distribution of coffee cultivation within each country. The ARIMAX order, though it now generalises well to the test period as the clean residual diagnostics confirm, was selected once on a single initial training window and within bounded search limits, leaving open whether a different window or a wider search would select a different specification. And all six models assume static predictor relationships over a 24-year period that witnessed substantial structural change in the coffee market.

These limitations point to several directions for future work. Cointegration-based error correction specifications could better handle the non-stationarity of the series while preserving the long-run equilibrium relationships among prices and fundamentals. Incorporating lagged climate variables at three, six and twelve months could allow the model to capture the delayed weather-to-price transmission channel that contemporaneous specifications cannot exploit, though the lagged COT check in this study is a reminder that such extensions do not always pay off and would need to be tested rather than assumed. Recurrent neural network architectures, in particular Long Short-Term Memory networks, could address the ANN's instability more fundamentally than any single fix tested in this study, by maintaining a hidden state across time steps rather than reinitialising at each walk-forward step. Testing the sensitivity of the ARIMAX order to the choice of initial training window could help establish how much of the strong Arabica result depends on the specific sample used. Finally, rolling-window or regime-switching specifications could allow predictor relationships to evolve over time, better reflecting the structural shifts the coffee market has undergone over the analysis period.

From a practical standpoint, the results suggest that market participants seeking short-run price signals for coffee would benefit most from monitoring speculative positioning in the futures market and energy prices rather than focusing on supply fundamentals or climate conditions at monthly frequency. The variety-specific results further suggest that Robusta-focused analysts should track supply conditions in the six countries identified in this study, chiefly Vietnam and Indonesia but also Uganda, Côte d'Ivoire, India and Brazil, as global aggregates dilute the variety-relevant signal. The consistent performance of multiple model families across both series and multiple specifications strengthens the reliability of these conclusions and suggests that the predictor set constructed in this study captures genuine and robust information about the drivers of coffee futures prices.

# Appendices

## Permutation Importance — Full Rankings

*The following plots report the full permutation importance rankings for all 14 predictors across the six models and both coffee varieties. Each bar represents the increase in MSE when the corresponding variable is randomly permuted on the test set.*

```{r importance_detailed_appendix, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}

options(scipen = 999)  # Force decimal notation, avoid scientific notation

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# DETAILED PERMUTATION IMPORTANCE PLOTS — APPENDICES
# All 14 variables are shown for each model and variety.
# Models are displayed in the same order as the document:
# MLR, ARIMAX, Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM, ANN.
# For MLR and ARIMAX, a note is added to the subtitle to
# remind the reader that their importance scores are not
# directly comparable to those of the ML models:
#   - MLR: severe multicollinearity causes negative scores
#   - ARIMAX: predicts in original price units, so scores
#     are several orders of magnitude larger than ML models
# Negative scores are kept here (unlike the main text plots)
# to show the full picture for each model.
# ----------------------------------------------------------


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — PLOT FUNCTION
# A single reusable function handles all 12 plots.
# geom_hline at zero helps distinguish positive from
# negative importance scores visually.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

plot_importance_appendix <- function(imp_df, color, bg_color,
                                      title, subtitle = NULL) {

  # Format labels: round to 4 decimal places for ML models,
  # round to 0 for ARIMAX which has very large values
  imp_df <- imp_df %>%
    mutate(label = ifelse(abs(Importance) > 100,
                          format(round(Importance, 0), big.mark = ","),
                          as.character(round(Importance, 4))))

  ggplot(imp_df, aes(x = reorder(Variable, Importance),
                     y = Importance)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity",
             fill = ifelse(imp_df$Importance >= 0, color, "grey70"),
             alpha = 0.85, width = 0.65) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey40",
               linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_text(aes(label = label),
              hjust = ifelse(imp_df$Importance >= 0, -0.15, 1.15),
              size = 3, color = "grey30") +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.2, 0.3))) +
    labs(title    = title,
         subtitle = subtitle,
         x = NULL, y = "ΔMSE") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
      panel.background   = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA),
      strip.background   = element_rect(fill = bg_color, color = NA),
      plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
      plot.subtitle      = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey50"),
      axis.text.y        = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey20"),
      axis.text.x        = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey40"),
      plot.margin = ggplot2::margin(10, 20, 10, 10)
    )
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — MLR
# All 14 variables shown. Grey bars indicate negative scores
# (permuting the variable improves forecast accuracy), which
# arise from severe multicollinearity among the predictors.

  imp_perm_mlr_ara, "#8B4513", "#f5ece6",
  "Permutation importance — MLR (Arabica)",
  "Grey bars: negative scores caused by multicollinearity"
)

plot_importance_appendix(
  imp_perm_mlr_rob, "#2E8B57", "#e8f5ec",
  "Permutation importance — MLR (Robusta)",
  "Grey bars: negative scores caused by multicollinearity"
)
```
